name: Mediabridge 14AWG Speaker Wire
summary: Affordable 14-gauge oxygen-free copper speaker wire with polarity markings and CL2-rated versions for in-wall runs; the sensible default for most 5.1 and 7.1 rooms.
verdict:
Mediabridge's 14AWG wire is the default answer for most home theaters: **14-gauge, 2-conductor, 99.9% oxygen-free copper**, with clear polarity markings, sold in spools including the common **100-foot** length. **CL2-rated** versions are available for running inside walls.

**Show the maths: how far can 14 AWG go?** Copper 14 AWG measures about **2.5 ohms per 1,000 feet**. A speaker run is a round trip (out and back), so a 50-foot run is 100 feet of conductor, or about **0.25 Ω**. A common rule is to keep wire resistance under **5% of the speaker's [impedance](/glossary/impedance/)**: 0.4 Ω for an 8-ohm speaker, 0.2 Ω for 4 ohms. That gives 14 AWG a comfortable limit of about **80 feet** to 8-ohm speakers and **40 feet** to 4-ohm speakers, which covers surround runs in almost any living room.

**How much do you need?** In a 15 × 20 ft room, front and center runs are short, but surround wires routed around the walls are often 20–30 feet each. A 5.1 system typically uses 80–100 feet including slack, so one 100-foot spool fits; a 7.1.4 layout with ceiling speakers usually needs more.

**In-wall rules.** Wire inside walls should carry a CL2 or CL3 rating for fire safety. Buy the CL2-rated version for those runs, not the standard spool.

Pair it with [Mediabridge banana plugs](/gear/mediabridge-banana-plugs/) for tidy connections. See the [best speaker wire for home theater](/best-speaker-wire-for-home-theater/) roundup.

name: Amazon Basics 16-Gauge Speaker Wire
amazonQuery: Amazon Basics 16 gauge speaker wire 100 feet
summary: Cheap, thin 16-gauge speaker wire that's fine for short runs to 8-ohm speakers, but too thin for long surround runs or 4-ohm loads.
verdict:
Amazon Basics 16-gauge wire is the cheapest way to hook up speakers: thin, flexible and easy to hide under rugs or along baseboards. It's sold in spools including **100 feet**, with a clear jacket and a polarity marking to keep positive and negative straight.

**Show the maths: 16 AWG has limits.** Copper 16 AWG measures about **4 ohms per 1,000 feet**. Because current travels out and back, a 30-foot run is 60 feet of conductor, or about **0.24 Ω**. Keeping wire resistance under **5% of the speaker's [impedance](/glossary/impedance/)** gives a limit of about **50 feet** to 8-ohm speakers and just **25 feet** to 4-ohm speakers. That's fine for front speakers a few feet from the receiver, but marginal for surrounds in a large room.

**Check the conductor.** Budget wire is sometimes copper-clad aluminum (CCA) rather than solid copper. CCA has roughly 1.6 times the resistance of copper, which makes 16 AWG CCA behave more like 18 AWG copper and cuts those run limits by about a third. Check the current listing before buying.

**In-wall use.** It isn't sold as CL2/CL3-rated, so don't run it inside walls.

For most rooms, 14 AWG such as [Mediabridge 14AWG](/gear/mediabridge-14awg-speaker-wire/) costs a little more and removes the guesswork. Use this for short front runs, bookshelf speakers on a desk or a bedroom system. See the [best speaker wire for home theater](/best-speaker-wire-for-home-theater/) roundup.

verdict:
GearIT sells 14AWG speaker wire in several versions, including **oxygen-free copper** "Pro Series" listings and **CL2/CL3-rated** versions for in-wall use, as well as cheaper copper-clad aluminum (CCA) options. That range is the catch: the right GearIT wire is excellent value, the wrong one is a different product.

**Show the maths: why the conductor matters.** Copper 14 AWG measures about **2.5 ohms per 1,000 feet**; CCA is roughly **1.6 times** higher, about 4 ohms, which is what **16 AWG copper** measures. Using the rule that wire resistance should stay under **5% of the speaker's [impedance](/glossary/impedance/)** (round trip):
- **Copper 14 AWG:** about **80 ft** to 8-ohm speakers, **40 ft** to 4-ohm.
- **CCA 14 AWG:** about **50 ft** to 8-ohm speakers, **25 ft** to 4-ohm.

For a typical living room the copper version handles every run; the CCA version is fine for front speakers but tighter for surrounds.

**In-wall.** Only use the CL2- or CL3-rated version inside walls. Standard spools aren't fire-rated for that.

**Handling.** Owners describe it as flexible and easy to strip, with clear polarity marking. If you'd rather not decode listings, [Mediabridge 14AWG](/gear/mediabridge-14awg-speaker-wire/) is the simpler pick. name: Monoprice 12AWG Speaker Wire
summary: Thick 12-gauge oxygen-free copper speaker wire for long runs and 4-ohm speakers; overkill for short runs, ideal for big rooms and in-wall installs.
verdict:
Monoprice's 12AWG speaker wire uses **oxygen-free pure bare copper** in a thick, 2-conductor cable, with **CL2-rated** versions for in-wall runs. It's the wire to use when runs get long or speakers dip to 4 ohms.

**Show the maths: when 12 AWG is worth it.** Copper 12 AWG measures about **1.6 ohms per 1,000 feet**, versus 2.5 for 14 AWG and 4.0 for 16 AWG. Keeping wire resistance below **5% of the speaker's [impedance](/glossary/impedance/)** (counting the round trip) gives these limits:

| Gauge | 8 Ω speakers | 4 Ω speakers |
|---|---|---|
| 12 AWG | ~125 ft | ~60 ft |
| 14 AWG | ~80 ft | ~40 ft |
| 16 AWG | ~50 ft | ~25 ft |

So 12 AWG makes sense for rear surrounds in a large dedicated room, ceiling speakers wired through the attic, or 4-ohm towers with long runs. For a 10-foot front run, it's audibly identical to 14 AWG.

**Installation reality.** Thick wire is harder to bend into tight spring clips, and many receivers' terminals are cramped. Banana plugs that accept 12 AWG, such as [Mediabridge banana plugs](/gear/mediabridge-banana-plugs/), make connections cleaner.

**In-wall.** Buy the CL2-rated version for inside walls.

Owners rate the copper quality and value highly. If your longest run is under 40 feet, [Mediabridge 14AWG](/gear/mediabridge-14awg-speaker-wire/) saves money. See the [best speaker wire for home theater](/best-speaker-wire-for-home-theater/) roundup.

faqs.a: Only on long runs where 14 AWG's resistance becomes significant. On short runs the difference is negligible.

name: KnuKonceptz Kord 12 Gauge Speaker Wire
summary: Flexible 12-gauge speaker wire from a car-audio brand, easy to route and terminate; check the listing for the conductor, since that sets how far it can run.
verdict:
KnuKonceptz is best known in car audio, where wire has to bend around tight corners, and its Kord 12-gauge speaker wire carries that flexibility into the home. Owners like how easy it is to route along baseboards and through tight spaces and how cleanly it strips and terminates compared with stiffer 12 AWG.

**Show the maths: copper vs CCA.** KnuKonceptz sells both oxygen-free copper and copper-clad aluminum (CCA) wire, so check what the current Kord listing uses. It changes the numbers:
- **Copper 12 AWG** is about **1.6 ohms per 1,000 feet**. Keeping wire resistance under **5% of the speaker's [impedance](/glossary/impedance/)** (round trip) allows about **125 ft** to 8-ohm speakers and **60 ft** to 4-ohm.
- **CCA 12 AWG** has roughly 1.6 times the resistance, which makes it perform like **14 AWG copper**: about **80 ft** to 8-ohm speakers and **40 ft** to 4-ohm.

Either way, that's plenty for most living rooms; it only matters in large rooms with 4-ohm speakers.

**Terminations.** Flexible, fine-stranded wire splays easily, so twist the strands tightly or use banana plugs like [Mediabridge banana plugs](/gear/mediabridge-banana-plugs/). It isn't sold primarily for in-wall use, so check for a CL rating before running it inside walls.

name: Mediabridge Banana Plugs (12 Pairs)
summary: A 12-pair pack of gold-plated screw-lock banana plugs that makes speaker connections tidier, more secure and easy to swap; enough for one end of a 7-speaker system.
verdict:
Banana plugs aren't about sound quality; they're about **secure, tidy, swappable connections**. Mediabridge's pack includes **12 pairs (24 plugs)** with gold-plated contacts and screw-lock terminals: strip the wire, insert it, tighten the screw and the plug pushes into any standard binding post.

**Count the plugs before buying.** Each speaker has two conductors. Terminating **both ends** of every wire takes **4 plugs per speaker**:
- 5.1 system: 5 speakers × 4 = **20 plugs** (the sub uses an RCA cable, so it needs none). One pack covers it.
- 7.1 system: 7 × 4 = **28 plugs**. One pack covers only one end; buy two or plug only the receiver side.
- 5.1.2 or 7.1.4: you'll need two packs if you want both ends done.

**Why they help.** Bare wire frays, strands short across terminals and oxidizes over time; a loose strand touching the opposite terminal can trip a receiver's protection circuit. Plugs prevent that and make swapping speakers or moving a receiver a one-minute job.

**Gauge fit.** Check that the plugs accept your wire. Thick 12 AWG like [Monoprice 12AWG](/gear/monoprice-12awg-speaker-wire/) fills the opening; trim stray strands so the screw clamps cleanly. They suit 14 AWG such as [Mediabridge 14AWG](/gear/mediabridge-14awg-speaker-wire/) easily.

Owners rate the build and fit for the price. See the [best speaker wire for home theater](/best-speaker-wire-for-home-theater/) roundup and the [home theater setup guide](/home-theater-setup-guide/).
